findings.claim: Filtering out q === 0 entries discards the negation information, so an explicitly rejected type can still be served via a surviving wildcard entry.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 12.5.1 uses q=0 not just to demote an entry but to exclude that media range. With `Accept: */*, text/html;q=0` the `text/html;q=0` entry is removed by the filter, leaving only `*/*`, which matchType will match against a supported `text/html`, returning exactly the type the client rejected. Correct handling requires keeping zero-q entries as an exclusion list checked against each candidate in `supports`, not filtering them away. Fairly confident this is a real gap, assuming matchType treats wildcards as matching (which getSpecificity implies).

findings.claim: `accept.q > 0` silently discards entries whose q is NaN or undefined, potentially emptying the whole candidate list.
findings.rationale: The declared type is `q: number`, but header parsers commonly yield NaN for malformed values like `q=abc`, and an entry with no q parameter may be left undefined depending on the parser. Both `NaN > 0` and `undefined > 0` are false, so such entries are dropped and the function falls through to defaultSupport, whereas previously they were still considered for matching. A defensive form such as `(accept.q ?? 1) > 0` or `!(accept.q <= 0)` would preserve prior behavior. Medium confidence; depends on the parser feeding this function.

findings.claim: When every accept entry has q=0, the loop now matches nothing and the function returns defaultSupport, serving content the client explicitly declared unacceptable.
findings.rationale: `Accept: */*;q=0` previously matched and returned a supported type; after this change sortedAccepts is empty and control falls through to the default return. Returning the default contradicts the stated intent that zero-q entries must never match - a 406 would arguably be required. Even if defaulting is the deliberate contract of this helper, callers relying on the previous match result see a silent behavior change worth covering in tests. Moderate confidence this is an unintended edge case.
